title: CHAPTER SEVEN. On the means of salvation; Word as law or Gospel
latin: CAPUT SEPTIMUM, De mediis salutis humanae, & quidem nominatim de lege. Hactenus vidimus de principiis salutis, e quibus ea dependet; nunc agemus de mediis, quibus ad eam pervenitur, eaque sunt alia externa, quibus a Deo salus aeterna nobis patefit et offertur, aliud internum, quo illa ab eodem nobis confertur & a nobis apprehenditur. II. Externa sunt: verbum, sacramenta & ministerium. III. VERBUM Dei est externum salutis medium, quo Deus hominibus voluntatem suam indicat, ut cognoscant quid ab ipsis fieri velit, & quomodo erga eos affectus sit. IV. Estque lex aut Evangelium. Totum Dei verbum libris V. & N.T. nunc continetur.
english: CHAPTER SEVEN. On the means of human salvation, and namely on the law.

Thus far we have seen the principles of salvation on which it depends; now we will treat the means by which one arrives at it. These are partly external, by which eternal salvation is opened and offered to us by God, and partly internal, by which it is conferred on us by the same God and apprehended by us.

II. The external means are: the word, the sacraments, and the ministry. III. The WORD of God is the external means of salvation by which God indicates His will to humans, so that they may know what He wills to be done by them and how He is affected toward them. IV. And it is law or Gospel. The whole word of God is now contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): On ye means belonging toward human salvation, and namely on ye law. — CHAPTER SEVEN. — These stand as partly external, by which eternal salvation stands as opened and offered toward us by God, and partly internal, by which it stands as conferred on us by ye same God and apprehended by us. — now we will treat ye means by which one arrives at it. — Thus far we have seen ye principles belonging toward salvation on which it depends; — Ye whole word belonging toward God stands as now contained in ye books belonging toward ye Old and New Testaments. — And it stands as law or Gospel. — IV. — Ye WORD belonging toward God stands as ye external means belonging toward salvation by which God indicates His will toward humans, so that they may know what He wills toward be done by them and how He stands as affected toward them. — III. — ye word, ye sacraments, and ye ministry. — Ye external means stand as: — II.

title: VI–X. Law defined; law of nature and human law
latin: VI. Sunt autem hic observandi distinctiones. Lex divina in se nihil aliud est quam idea voluntatis divinae de rebus agendis & omittendis. Lex Dei requirit obedientiam perfectam omnibusque viribus; non tantum ordinat actiones hominis, verum etiam vetat actiones quibus aliis peccandi occasio datur. VII. Est autem lex vel naturae, vel humana, vel divina. VIII. Lex NATURAE est lumen & dictamen rectae rationis, quo homo naturaliter discernit honestum a turpi. Lex naturae, qualis jam est in hominibus post lapsum, scintillas quasdam adhuc retinet quibus peccatum redarguitur. X. Lex humana est definita iuris sententia a magistratu lata ad regendam societatem civilem.
english: VI. Distinctions are to be observed here. The divine law in itself is nothing other than the idea of the divine will concerning things to be done and omitted. The law of God requires perfect obedience with all powers; it not only orders the human's actions but also forbids actions by which occasion of sinning is given to others.

VII. Law is either of nature, or human, or divine. VIII. The law of NATURE is the light and dictate of right reason by which a human naturally discerns the honorable from the base. The law of nature as it now is in humans after the fall still retains certain sparks by which sin is rebuked.
X. Human law is a definite sentence of right issued by the magistrate for governing civil society.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): it not only orders ye human's actions but also forbids actions by which occasion belonging toward sinning stands as given toward others. — Ye law belonging toward God requires perfect obedience with all powers; — Ye divine law in itself stands as nothing other than ye idea belonging toward ye divine will concerning things toward be done and omitted. — Distinctions stand as toward be observed here. — VI. — Ye law belonging toward nature as it now stands as in humans after ye fall still retains certain sparks by which sin stands as rebuked. — Ye law belonging toward NATURE stands as ye light and dictate belonging toward right reason by which a human naturally discerns ye honorable from ye base. — VIII. — Law stands as either belonging toward nature, or human, or divine. — VII. — Human law stands as a definite sentence belonging toward right issued by ye magistrate toward governing civil society. — X.

title: XI–XVI. Divine moral law and the Decalogue's two tables
latin: XI. Lex DIVINA est definita sententia Dei in scripturis proposita. XIII. Lex MORALIS est quae praecipit officia perpetua erga Deum & proximum, in Decalogo summatim comprehensa. XIV. Hujus legis DECEM VERBA sunt summa totius moralitatis. XV. Est itaque lex moralis distincta in duas tabulas. XVI. Prior tabula quatuor praeceptis officia erga Deum continet; posterior tabula sex praeceptis officia erga proximum.
english: XI. Divine law is a definite sentence of God proposed in the Scriptures. XIII. Moral law is that which commands perpetual duties toward God and neighbor, summarily comprehended in the Decalogue.

XIV. The TEN WORDS of this law are the sum of all morality. XV. The moral law is therefore distinguished into two tables. XVI. The former table contains duties toward God in four precepts; the latter table contains duties toward the neighbor in six precepts.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Moral law stands as that which commands perpetual duties toward God and neighbor, summarily comprehended in ye Decalogue. — XIII. — Divine law stands as a definite sentence belonging toward God proposed in ye Scriptures. — XI. — ye latter table contains duties toward ye neighbor in six precepts. — Ye former table contains duties toward God in four precepts; — XVI. — Ye moral law stands as therefore distinguished into two tables. — XV. — Ye TEN WORDS belonging toward this law stand as ye sum belonging toward all morality. — XIV.

title: XVII–XXIV. First table: duties toward God
latin: XVII–XXIV. Prioris tabulae praecepta exigunt Dei notitiam, amorem, timorem, fiduciam & cultum internum & externum; vetant idololatriam, abusum nominis Dei & violationem sabbati. Imagines Dei ad cultum prohibentur; historicae imagines, modo ad cultum aut scandalum non prostituantur, non prorsus vetantur. Verba ad religionem relata tertio praecepto sanctificantur. Officia solennia cultus publici & privati quarto praecepto continentur.
english: XVII–XXIV. The precepts of the former table require knowledge, love, fear, trust, and worship of God, internal and external; they forbid idolatry, abuse of God's name, and violation of the sabbath.

Images of God for worship are prohibited; historical images, provided they are not prostituted to worship or scandal, are not altogether forbidden. Words related to religion are sanctified by the third precept. Solemn duties of public and private worship are contained in the fourth precept.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): they forbid idolatry, abuse belonging toward God's name, and violation belonging toward ye sabbath. — Ye precepts belonging toward ye former table require knowledge, love, fear, trust, and worship belonging toward God, internal and external; — XVII–XXIV. — Solemn duties belonging toward public and private worship stand as contained in ye fourth precept. — Words related toward religion stand as sanctified by ye third precept. — historical images, provided they stand as not prostituted toward worship or scandal, stand as not altogether forbidden. — Images belonging toward God toward worship stand as prohibited;

title: XXV–XXXIV. Second table: duties toward neighbor
latin: XXV. Posterior tabula sex praeceptis officia erga proximum praescribit, quae Christus summa charitatis complexus est: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. XXVIII. Officia quae actiones circa ordinem humanae societatis respiciunt quinto praecepto praescribuntur, ut alii praesint, alii subsint. Sequuntur praecepta de vita, conjugio, bonis, & loquela: non occides, non moechaberis, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces. XXXIV. Hucusque fuere officia quae lex moralis praescribit.
english: XXV. The latter table with six precepts prescribes duties toward the neighbor, which Christ comprehended in the sum of charity: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

XXVIII. Duties that regard actions around the order of human society are prescribed by the fifth precept, so that some preside and others are subject. There follow the precepts concerning life, marriage, goods, and speech: you shall not kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet.
XXXIV. Thus far were the duties that the moral law prescribes.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): You shall love your neighbor as yourself. — Ye latter table with six precepts prescribes duties toward ye neighbor, which Christ comprehended in ye sum belonging toward charity: — XXV. — you shall not kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet. — There follow ye precepts concerning life, marriage, goods, and speech: — Duties that regard actions around ye order belonging toward human society stand as prescribed by ye fifth precept, so that some preside and others stand as subject. — XXVIII. — Thus far were ye duties that ye moral law prescribes. — XXXIV.

title: XXXV–XXXVII. Uses of the moral law before and after the fall
latin: XXXV. Est autem in lege morali notandus usus & abrogatio. XXXVI. Usus legis moralis variat secundum status hominis. Usus legis moralis in statu integritatis fuit norma perfectae obedientiae. XXXVI–XXXVII. Usus legis moralis erga homines post lapsum est 1. ut peccatorum suorum convincat, Rom. 3:19-20; 4:15; 7:7; 2. ut sit paedagogus ad Christum, Gal. 3:24; 3. ut sit nuncia iusti iudicii Dei adversus eos tandem exercendi; 4. ut renatis sit norma vitae.
english: XXXV. In the moral law the use and abrogation are to be noted. XXXVI. The use of the moral law varies according to the human's state. In the state of integrity its use was the norm of perfect obedience.

After the fall its use toward humans is: 1. that it may convict them of their sins (Rom. 3:19-20; 4:15; 7:7); 2. that it may be a pedagogue to Christ (Gal. 3:24); 3. that it may be a herald of the just judgment of God finally to be exercised against them; 4. that for the regenerate it may be a norm of life.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): In ye state belonging toward integrity its use was ye norm belonging toward perfect obedience. — Ye use belonging toward ye moral law varies according toward ye human's state. — XXXVI. — In ye moral law ye use and abrogation stand as toward be noted. — XXXV. — that toward ye regenerate it may be a norm belonging toward life. — 4. — that it may be a herald belonging toward ye just judgment belonging toward God finally toward be exercised against them; — 3. — 3:24); — that it may be a pedagogue toward Christ (Gal. — 2. — 7:7); — 4:15; — 3:19-20; — that it may convict them belonging toward their sins (Rom. — 1. — After ye fall its use toward humans stands as:

title: XXXVIII–XXXIX. How far the moral law is abrogated for believers
latin: XXXVIII. Abrogatio legis moralis quousque pertineat, & quousque obtineat inter fideles sub gratia Christi constitutos, ex usibus iam propositis facile colligitur. Nam 1. abrogata est quantum ad primum usum iustificandi; 2. quantum ad maledictionem & condemnationem; 3. quantum ad acuendum peccatum in omnem concupiscentiam; 4. quantum ad rigorem & modum ducendi hominem in obsequium. XXXIX. Obedientiae vero quam lex exigit substantia manet, etsi modus & rigor iustificationis legalis cessavit sub Evangelio.
english: XXXVIII. How far the abrogation of the moral law extends, and how far it obtains among the faithful constituted under the grace of Christ, is easily gathered from the uses already set out. For 1. it is abrogated as to the first use of justifying; 2. as to curse and condemnation; 3. as to sharpening sin into all concupiscence; 4. as to the rigor and mode of leading a human into obedience.
XXXIX. But the substance of the obedience that the law demands remains, even if the mode and rigor of legal justification has ceased under the Gospel.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): as toward ye rigor and mode belonging toward leading a human into obedience. — 4. — as toward sharpening sin into all concupiscence; — 3. — as toward curse and condemnation; — 2. — it stands as abrogated as toward ye first use belonging toward justifying; — For 1. — How far ye abrogation belonging toward ye moral law extends, and how far it obtains among ye faithful constituted under ye grace belonging toward Christ, stands as easily gathered from ye uses already set out. — XXXVIII. — But ye substance belonging toward ye obedience that ye law demands remains, even if ye mode and rigor belonging toward legal justification has ceased under ye Gospel. — XXXIX.

title: Canons of interpreting the Decalogue; Cap.8 next on ceremonial law
latin: In affirmatione negatio, & in negatione affirmatio opposita comprehenditur, quia Deus non solum abstinentiam a malo verum etiam efficientiam boni postulat. Actiones homogeneae & cognatae eodem praecepto iubentur aut vetantur. Effectus in sua causa, & causa in suo effectu iubetur & prohibetur. Relativo uno praecepto vel prohibito, etiam alterum praecipitur vel prohibetur. Si contingat duorum praeceptorum observationem simul praestari non posse, eius habetur ratio quod momenti maioris est. CAPUT OCTAVUM sequitur, De lege cerimoniali.
english: In an affirmation the opposite negation is comprehended, and in a negation the opposite affirmation, because God demands not only abstinence from evil but also the doing of good. Homogeneous and related actions are commanded or forbidden by the same precept. An effect is commanded and forbidden in its cause, and a cause in its effect. When one relative is commanded or forbidden by a precept, the other also is commanded or forbidden. If it happens that two precepts cannot be observed at once, regard is had to that which is of greater moment.
CHAPTER EIGHT follows, On the ceremonial law.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): If it happens that two precepts cannot be observed at once, regard stands as had toward that which stands as belonging toward greater moment. — When one relative stands as commanded or forbidden by a precept, ye other also stands as commanded or forbidden. — An effect stands as commanded and forbidden in its cause, and a cause in its effect. — Homogeneous and related actions stand as commanded or forbidden by ye same precept. — In an affirmation ye opposite negation stands as comprehended, and in a negation ye opposite affirmation, because God demands not only abstinence from evil but also ye doing belonging toward good. — CHAPTER EIGHT follows, On ye ceremonial law.
